preamble: Glide formation turns the close front vowel [i] into the palatal approximant [j] before another vowel. Between Classical Latin and Proto-Romance, unstressed front vowels in hiatus became /j/ (fīlius > /ˈfiːljus/), and so did stressed ones in the antepenult, with the stress moving to the following vowel (fīliolus > /fiːˈljolus/). French has the same process synchronically: a verb stem ending in /i/ has [j] before a vowel-initial ending (nie [ni], nier [nje]), but not after an obstruent + liquid onset.

examples.note: The stressed i of the antepenult also became /j/, and the stress moved to the following vowel.

languageExamples.context: Before a vowel, except after an obstruent + liquid onset

examples.note: Wikipedia analyses the glide as an underlying high vowel before another vowel: /nie/ → [nje].
